title: Trump talks turkey, and his ballroom, at pardoning event
source: Axios — Trump talks turkey, and his ballroom, at pardoning event (2026-11-24)
body: President Trump honored a time-worn Washington tradition Tuesday: pardoning poultry — after using the pulpit to praise his White House ballroom and deliver a rally-reminiscent speech. The big picture: Freedom and Feathers, this year's honored birds, continue a bizarre American tradition officially dating back to 1989 — but building on far older presidential lore. Driving the news: "Unfortunately, for 200 years, the White House lacked appropriate accommodations to host such distinguished guests," Trump said at the event, held on the White House's South Lawn. He continued, "I'm pleased to announce that next year we'll be able to have a special location right over there in that rather small ballroom being built." Trump's hotly contested project will be a 90,000-square-foot addition, far larger than the main White House. "I've heard better," he said about the birds' names, though they still earned presidential pardons. Both birds will dodge the oven and retire at Texas A&M University. State of play: The collective 82 pounds of white-feathered flamboyance traveled from West Virginia's Deans Gap Farm for the event. Pointing to his large 2024 election win in West Virginia, Trump said Tuesday, "I won it by a lot. I don't know what the hell happened with this last election. Somebody, please explain it to me." The pair are just four months old. Per a White House fact sheet , Freedom's favorite treat is Dr. Pepper. Feathers prefers to snack on Golden Delicious apples, which — like the turkeys — hail from West Virginia. Between the lines: Trump has never shied away from using the event to ruffle feathers. Last year, he jabbed at former President Biden and attacked Chicago leadership, derailing the focus on his feathered guests by calling Gov. JB Pritzker (D) a "fat slob." During his first term, he joked that the turkeys trotting before him had were slated to "appear in Adam Schiff's basement," a nod to the Democrat who led the 2019 impeachment inquiry into Trump. While Trump has taken presidential rhetoric to a new level, he's not the first to have stuffed political zingers into the bizarre tradition. In 2022, Biden seemingly poked fun at Trump's false claim he'd won the 2020 election, saying : "The votes are in. They've been counted and verified. There's no ballot stuffing. There's no fowl play." Worth noting: PETA called on the White House to end the event, saying presidents are "conned every year into becoming the unpaid spokesperson for factory farmers." President Tracy Reiman called the idea of retirement for the birds "all squawk, no substance, " noting fattened-up turkeys often die prematurely. Flashback: While George H.W. Bush formalized the pardon in 1989, the White House's quirky turkey ties stretch back well over a century. Abraham Lincoln is frequently credited with sparing the first turkey on record at the urging of his son in the 1860s, according to the White House Historical Association. Harry Truman welcomed a live turkey from the National Turkey Federation in 1947, and the photo-op was hatched. But that bird wasn't such a lucky duck — perhaps becoming part of the Thanksgiving feast. Since then, the NTF has presented the presidential bird. And President John F. Kennedy was gifted a turkey in 1963, but decided instead to "let this one grow." The bottom line: Through decades of conflict, campaigns and chaos, presidents have come face-to-beak with the ubiquitous Thanksgiving birds. Go deeper: The turkey pardon: A quirky White House custom
